history.title: Take It Apart

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Most bad arguments are not lies. They are true facts stapled to a claim they do not actually support. This week you learn to spot the gap, and to stop leaving one in your own writing.

1. Read **Says Who?**
2. Learn the words in **Argument Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three Parts, Two Gaps** chart open while you read anything.
4. Trace **How an Argument Holds Together** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Claim, Evidence, or Reasoning?**
6. Use the **Argument Frames** out loud before you write.
7. Take **Argument Check**.
8. Lock it in with **Remember the Three Parts**.
9. Read **Argument Questions Kids Ask**.
10. Finish with **Decide: Which Argument Should the School Act On?**

Your job this week: find one real argument — an advert, a headline, a group chat — and name its three parts, or say which one is missing. 🧩

Sort by each sentence’s stated role in the three fictional proposals. All numbers here are invented classroom data. An evidence statement can also be a factual assertion outside its supporting role.

history.title: Says Who?
history.data:
## Says Who?

“We should keep the library open until five.” This is a **claim**: a statement the writer wants us to accept. It calls for an action. A claim can also be about a **fact**, such as the library's closing time. Facts and claims are not opposites.

An **argument** gives support for a claim. **Evidence** is information used as support. It can be a record, an observation, an example or an exact quote. **Reasoning** explains how the evidence supports the claim. It also shows the limits of that link.

Try this made-up case. A school has 120 students in one year group. In a week, a librarian records 40 different students using the library after three. These are invented numbers for practice, not research results.

A writer wants later opening hours. Forty is one third of 120. The record shows that some students use the library after school. It does not show that all 40 want to stay until five. It also says nothing about staffing costs. The writer needs more evidence for those points.

Here is another made-up case. Six of eleven team members have a fixed plan on Tuesdays. That supports a claim that Tuesday practice is hard for many to attend. It does not show that Thursday is better. Check their plans for Thursday too. Reasoning cannot take the place of missing evidence.

A **counterclaim** is an opposing claim. A person may also question the evidence or the link between it and the claim. Give a fair account of a strong objection. A **rebuttal** responds with reasons and evidence. It may admit a limit or lead the writer to change the claim.

A fact is something that is the case. A statement that claims to be a fact still needs checking. An **opinion** is a belief, judgment or preference. An opinion about school policy can have good reasons behind it. Calling it an opinion does not settle the debate.

Evidence is **relevant** when it bears on the exact claim. The wall color will not settle how late the library should stay open. Check the **source**, how the information was gathered, and what else might explain it. Check arguments you agree with too.

In the sort, read each statement's role in its made-up case. A statement can serve as evidence even though someone is also claiming it is true. Use the words as well as the picture.

history.title: Argument Words

data.def: A reasoned case offering support for a claim.
A statement someone wants others to accept. It can be about a fact, a value or an action.
Information used to support a claim. Check whether it is sound and fits the question.
An explanation of how evidence supports a claim and where that link has limits.
A claim that opposes another claim.
Something that is the case. Check the evidence for a statement that claims to be a fact.
A belief, judgment or preference. It may have reasons behind it.
Related to the exact claim or question being discussed.
Where information comes from, such as a person, text or record.
A response to an opposing claim or objection, backed by reasons.

history.title: Claim, Evidence, or Reasoning?

items.content: Library proposal: the library should stay open until five.
Cooking proposal: the school should offer a basic cooking club.
Team proposal: our team should practise on Thursdays instead.
Fictional library record offered as support: 40 of the year group’s 120 students used the library after three last week.
Fictional cooking survey offered as support: 19 of 28 respondents said they would join a cooking club.
Fictional team record offered as support: six of eleven players report a fixed commitment on Tuesdays.
Library explanation: serving one third of the year group suggests after-school access matters, though we still need demand data for later hours.
Team explanation: when many players cannot attend, changing the time could improve participation; Thursday availability still needs checking.
Cooking explanation: expressed interest suggests a club could attract participants, but interest alone does not establish cost or attendance.

history.meta: 6 frames • say them out loud before writing • rubric included

items.text: The evidence offered is ____, which came from ____.
This evidence supports the claim because ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Evaluator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finding the parts | Names the topic | Names claim and evidence | Names claim, evidence and reasoning, and quotes each |
| Testing the link | Accepts the evidence | Says whether it is relevant | Shows a different conclusion the same evidence would fit |
| The other side | Not mentioned | States an objection | States the strongest objection fairly, then answers it |

history.title: Argument Check

questions.question: Fictional argument: “Keep the library open until five. Forty students used it after three.” What is missing?
options: A link from current use to later hours, with limits
A description of a policy the writer wants adopted
A record showing that students use the library
Nothing; current use settles the best closing time
questions.correctAnswer: A link from current use to later hours, with limits

questions.question: Which statement proposes an action rather than asserting a current fact?
options: The posted opening time is 8:15
The timetable lists a bus at 7:52
The record lists 62 student visits
The library should stay open later
questions.correctAnswer: The library should stay open later

questions.question: What does it mean for evidence to be relevant?
options: It comes from a source that is recent and well known
It is interesting enough to keep the reader's attention
It bears on this particular claim, not just the topic
It is a number rather than a story or a quotation
questions.correctAnswer: It bears on this particular claim, not just the topic

questions.question: What can a well-supported response to a relevant counterclaim do?
options: Make all readers agree with the claim
Remove the need to check the evidence
Explain how it handles a serious objection
Prove that every opposing view is false
questions.correctAnswer: Explain how it handles a serious objection

questions.question: Which is the most thorough way to evaluate support?
options: Trust familiar sources and ignore other accounts
Check sources, relevance, reasoning and other explanations
Count examples without checking how they were gathered
Trust the evidence that appears first in the argument
questions.correctAnswer: Check sources, relevance, reasoning and other explanations

questions.question: Fictional argument: “We should ban phones at lunch. Our survey reports increased phone use.” Identify the claim and offered evidence, and explain what still needs checking.
questions.expectedAnswer: The claim recommends a lunchtime ban. The offered evidence is a reported increase in use. Check the survey and whether it concerns lunch, explain the claimed problem, and evaluate evidence about the proposed response. An increase alone does not establish that a ban would help.

questions.question: Write a claim you agree with, then state the strongest objection to it as fairly as you can.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer states an arguable claim, then gives an objection a thoughtful opponent would actually make, phrased without mockery or a weakened version, showing the student can represent the other side accurately.

reflections.text: What is an argument you have heard recently that had evidence but no reasoning?
Was it harder to state the objection fairly than you expected? Why?

history.title: Argument Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is an opinion just a weak claim? 🤔
data.answer: An opinion can be a belief, judgment or preference. It can have good reasons behind it. A claim may be about a fact or an action, so facts and claims are not opposites.

data.question: Can evidence be true and still be bad evidence?
data.answer: Yes. A true detail may not help answer the question. First check that it is true. Then ask how it supports this claim.

data.question: Does more evidence always make an argument stronger? 📊
data.answer: No. Check the quality and fit of the evidence. A pile of weak examples may still leave a gap.

data.question: What if I cannot find a counterclaim?
data.answer: Look for a serious objection or another way to explain the evidence. Do not invent an equal case for both sides when the evidence does not support that.

data.question: Is it fine to argue for something I do not believe? 🎭
data.answer: A class task may ask you to study a view you do not hold. Explain it fairly. Make clear that it is an exercise, and do not make up support.

data.question: Do adults get this wrong too?
data.answer: Yes. People of any age can miss a weak link. Check the specific argument and its evidence.

history.meta: 6th Grade • Decision brief • judge the arguing, not the outcome

data.title: Which Argument Should the School Act On?
data.instructions: Four groups want the same money. Judge the arguments, not the causes. Recommend one, and be able to say why the best-argued case was not necessarily the one you liked.
data.fitReason: RI.6.8 asks students to distinguish claims supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not. Forcing a single recommendation from four proposals makes that distinction consequential instead of an exercise.

brief.context:
Classroom practice: one grant can fund one of four plans. All records below are made up. Judge the arguments as written. A real decision would need checked costs and more facts.
A. Library: Try keeping it open until five. A made-up log lists 40 of 120 students after three in one week. That shows some demand. A trial could check later demand and staff costs.
B. Sports: Buy new equipment. A made-up list has 50 club members. The writer says this proves the purchase is the best use of the grant.
C. Cooking: Try a club. In a made-up survey, 19 of 28 people said they would join. That suggests interest. The school still needs to check actual attendance, access, adult help and costs.
D. Rehearsal: Pay for an extra session. The writer says music is best, so everyone will gain.
Choose the best-supported case. Name what is still missing. This is not a final real-world budget decision.
brief.audience: A simulated school panel that needs a reasoned recommendation
brief.drivingQuestion: Which plan has the strongest argument? Is it also the plan you prefer?
brief.seedDirection: For each plan, list the claim, evidence and reasoning. Mark anything missing. Then rate the support.
lockedLessonFacts: Claims can concern facts, values or proposed actions.
Evidence must be relevant, reliable and sufficient for the conclusion.
Reasoning explains the link and its limitations.
A counterclaim is an opposing claim, and a rebuttal responds.
openQuestions: Could the same evidence support a different claim?
Does a writer deal with a strong objection?
Did your own preference affect your rating?
stakeholders: The four groups who wrote the proposals
Students who benefit from whichever wins
criteria: Identify the claim, evidence and reasoning in each plan. Mark missing parts.
Rate each plan and how it deals with an objection.
Choose one plan and explain why its argument is strongest.
Say whether it is also the plan you prefer.
Use at least four glossary words correctly.
constraints: Judge the argument as written, not what the group meant
Quote a supporting line for each rating, or state that the required support is absent
brief.deliverable: Make a table for the four plans. List each claim, evidence, reasoning and rating. Choose one, explain why, and name a limit. State your own preference.

parallelExample.context: Invented example: a panel initially prefers the sports proposal.
parallelExample.move: The panel notices that participation alone does not establish an equipment need. It compares the library and cooking proposals’ explanations and limitations before making a provisional recommendation.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They separated the quality of the case from the appeal of the cause, which is what the panel was actually asked to judge.

supports.frameStarter: Proposal ____ claims ____. Its evidence is ____. Its reasoning ____. I rate it ____ because ____.
coachPrompts: Did you write down the parts before you formed a view?
Which proposal's evidence would fit a different conclusion?
Is your recommendation also your favourite? Say so either way.

data.coachHint: Score the arguing first. Notice your preference second.
